c.tagline: Rum, reggae rhythms, and turquoise Caribbean shores.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are unmetered; agree the fare with the driver before departure or use published fixed-rate zones (e.g., airport to Bridgetown).

emergency.note: Fire: 311. Mobile 911 often routes to emergency services as well.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

hood_landmark.St. Lawrence Gap: St. Lawrence Gap, Christ Church, Barbados

avoid.reason: Avoid the Nelson Street area and lower Bridgetown's back streets after dark, a red-light pocket with drug activity and petty crime.
Keep valuables off the sand when swimming at Carlisle Bay and expect persistent (mostly harmless) vendor and taxi hustle around the cruise terminal.

hood_desc: A convenient south-coast strip midway between Bridgetown and the airport, with condos, boardwalk beaches, and budget-to-mid hotels; suits travelers wanting proximity to both the capital and the beach without luxury prices.
The island's liveliest stretch of restaurants, bars, and nightclubs packed along a walkable south-coast strip; suits younger travelers and anyone prioritizing nightlife and dining.
An upscale west-coast ("Platinum Coast") town with calm turquoise water, boutique resorts, and fine dining; suits honeymooners and travelers wanting a quieter, higher-end base.
A relaxed, budget-friendly south-coast neighborhood with a lagoon-calm beach and easy bus access to Bridgetown and the Gap; suits backpackers and value-conscious visitors.
The historic UNESCO-listed capital and adjoining Garrison area, home to the cruise port, museums, and the Garrison Savannah; suits history buffs and travelers who want to be near downtown sights.

water.note: Filtered through coral limestone and treated to WHO standards; one of the safest taps in the Caribbean.

transit.pay: Flat fare paid in cash directly to the driver/conductor on Transport Board buses (exact change preferred); ZR vans and private minibuses also charge a flat cash fare. There is no widely used integrated fare card for visitors.
transit.hours: Transport Board buses generally run about 5:30am-9pm on main routes with reduced frequency at night; ZR vans and minibuses often run later, especially on weekends, though options thin out after dark.
transit.note: No passenger rail on the island; getting beyond Bridgetown and the south coast typically means bus, ZR van, taxi, rideshare, or rental car.

tip.r: A 10% service charge is often added to restaurant bills in lieu of tipping; rounding up or a small extra tip for taxis, hotel staff, and great service is appreciated but not obligatory.

landmarks: Garrison Savannah
This UNESCO World Heritage former British military garrison combines historic forts and cannons with an active horse-racing track, blending colonial history with lively local sport.
St. Michael's Cathedral
The Cathedral Church of St. Michael and All Angels, dating to the 18th century, is a stately coral-stone landmark and the spiritual heart of Barbados's Anglican community.
Parliament Buildings
These neo-Gothic buildings house one of the oldest parliaments in the Western Hemisphere, their stained-glass windows and clock tower forming an iconic Bridgetown silhouette.
Chamberlain Bridge
Spanning the Careenage in the heart of downtown, this swing bridge is a picturesque focal point framed by yachts, waterfront restaurants, and the historic city center.
The Careenage
This historic inlet harbor, once used to careen and repair sailing ships, is now a scenic waterfront promenade lined with boats, cafes, and colonial architecture.
Nidhe Israel Synagogue
One of the oldest synagogues in the Western Hemisphere, this beautifully restored 17th-century building and adjoining cemetery tell the story of Barbados's early Jewish settlers.
George Washington House
The only house outside the United States ever lived in by George Washington, this restored 18th-century plantation home offers a fascinating window into colonial Barbados.
National Heroes Square
Formerly Trafalgar Square, this central plaza honors Barbados's national heroes and independence with fountains and monuments surrounded by the island's key civic buildings.
Kensington Oval
Barbados's legendary cricket stadium has hosted World Cup finals and legendary matches, making it a pilgrimage site for cricket fans visiting the island.
Independence Square
This waterfront square near the Careenage commemorates Barbados's 1966 independence and forms part of the historic Bridgetown UNESCO World Heritage core.

train.note: Barbados has no railway — the old Bridgetown-to-Belleplaine line closed in 1937. Get around by public bus, private ZR vans and minibuses, or taxi.

bus.note: Barbados is an island with no international coach routes. Islandwide transport is run by the government Transport Board (transportboard.com), the blue buses, plus privately-owned yellow minibuses and white ZR vans; most routes radiate from Bridgetown's Fairchild Street and Princess Alice terminals.

ferry.note: There is no scheduled international passenger ferry from Barbados as of mid-2026. A regional service (Connect Caribé / a CARICOM-backed ferry linking the Eastern Caribbean) is still in the planning and trial stage, not yet carrying passengers. Bridgetown Port handles cruise ships and cargo only; travel to other islands is by air.
